claims.text: At Linktree, as of February 2025, Devin authored approximately 300 pull requests over one month, of which about 100 were successfully merged (roughly a one-third merge rate).

Linktree's Devin contributions included bug fixes, small features, and initial implementations of more complex functionality, such as end-to-end integration of RedNote and Lemon8 across backend systems, URL handling, and UI components.

Cognition's Listen Labs case study reports that user research doubled the percentage of users who progressed from landing page to merging a PR with Devin (2x activation rate), with onboarding improvements shipped in a two-week sprint.
Devin operates in a cloud-based sandbox with its own Linux shell, code editor, browser, and standard developer tools.

When given a task via chat, the web platform, or Slack, Devin formulates a step-by-step plan, executes code, runs tests, debugs, and updates its plan as needed, streaming updates and accepting user corrections.
Cloud Devin has an Ask mode for planning together with the user and an Agent mode for autonomous execution.
Devin 2.0 added an interactive planning step where users can review and edit Devin's plan before coding starts, which reduces wasted ACUs on misunderstood requirements.
Repositories must be indexed before the first Devin session so Devin understands the codebase.
Devin automatically looks for an AGENTS.md file with setup commands, code standards, test requirements, and development workflow before starting work.
Devin's Knowledge stores project- or organization-wide guidance that is retrieved automatically only when relevant, rather than loaded fully into every context.
Devin Playbooks bundle reusable procedures for recurring tasks, and scheduled sessions plus playbooks support recurring quality checks.
The Devin CLI does not yet support Knowledge, Playbooks, or Secrets from a Devin account, according to the documentation.
The Devin CLI sandbox restricts write access to granted paths and refuses to start rather than run unsandboxed if sandbox resolution fails.
The Devin CLI can define custom subagents as Markdown files under agents/, running in the foreground or background.
A cloud Devin agent runs in its own infrastructure and environment for minutes or hours, opens PRs, runs tests, and QAs its own work using computer vision.
In Windsurf 2.0, a user plans locally in Windsurf, sends the plan to Devin with one click, Devin spins up its own machine, and the resulting PR is reviewed inside Windsurf.
Idlen claims Devin runs 4-12 hour sessions without human intervention (a secondary-source claim, not a Cognition publication).
Cognition says every Devin session is fully observable, with a timeline of every command and file touched, and that its orchestration layer runs thousands of agents concurrently.

Devin performs best on well-scoped, verifiable tasks (bug fixes, tests, dependency updates, boilerplate) and struggles with ambiguous requirements, large architectural decisions, and tasks needing mid-task human judgment.
A key Devin failure mode is cost unpredictability: an unclear brief can make a 3-hour task cost far more than expected, with 1 ACU being about 15 minutes of work at $2.25 on Core.
Troubleshooting guidance for Devin: if a PR fails CI, comment with the failure details so an active session can fix it, or start a new session for closed ones.
When Devin appears stuck or going in circles, the guidance is to intervene via chat with more specific guidance or break the task into smaller steps.
Large codebases and complex tasks consume more ACUs than expected; the guidance is to give clear scope boundaries such as specific files or functions.
Enterprise teams reportedly told analysts that Devin resolves security vulnerabilities in 1.5 minutes per issue versus 30 minutes for a human (a vendor-adjacent claim about well-structured tasks).
A Devin Desktop review notes that current documentation does not establish the defect rate of code produced by agent sessions or how accurately agents use shared context on difficult tasks.
